metadata.title: Charaka Samhita - Sutra Sthana
metadata.description: Sutra Sthana is the first section dealing with fundamental principles of Ayurveda. It consists of thirty chapters, grouped into eight logical contexts (Chatushkas). The word Sutra literally means a short sentence which has deep meaning. This section lays the foundation for the whole Samhita by describing the basic principles.

chatushkas.name: Swastha Chatushka
chatushkas.description: Four chapters on preservation of health

chatushkas.name: Nirdesha Chatushka
chatushkas.description: Four chapters on guidelines for healthcare management

chatushkas.name: Kalpana Chatushka
chatushkas.description: Four chapters on therapeutic purification procedures

chatushkas.name: Roga Chatushka
chatushkas.description: Four chapters on classification of diseases

chatushkas.name: Yojana Chatushka
chatushkas.description: Four chapters on guidelines for management of diseases

chatushkas.name: Annapana Chatushka
chatushkas.description: Four chapters on food and beverages

chapters.abstract: The title of Charak Samhita's the very first chapter, Deerghanjiviteeya Adhyaya, literally means the chapter on longevity. This is symbolic, because it implies that Ayurveda is not merely the science of life, but also a science of longevity. This chapter deliberates on the purpose of long life and health as the means of achieving the four primary instincts of human beings (purushartha chatustaya). These are virtue (dharma), wealth (artha), gratification (kama) and emancipation (moksha). Some of the basic tenets of Ayurveda and its scope are explained. The chapter introduces fundamental principles of Ayurveda, including its definition, objective, concept of three sharira (bodily) dosha and their qualities, and two manasa (mental) dosha and their treatment. The theory of similarity (samanya) and dissimilarity (vishesha), pharmaco-therapeutic aspects, classification of drugs, list of herbs and other animal products useful in purification and pacification therapies are highlighted.
keyConcepts: Plant origin drugs - roots, fruits, latex, bark
importantVerses: Verse 41: Definition of Ayurveda - हिताहितं सुखं दुःखमायुस्तस्य हिताहितम्। मानं च तच्च यत्रोक्तमायुर्वेदः स उच्यते।।
Verse 42: Definition of Ayu - शरीरेन्द्रियसत्त्वात्मसंयोगो धारि जीवितं। नित्यगश्चानुबन्धश्च पर्यायैरायुरुच्यते।।
Verse 44: Samanya Vishesha - सर्वदा सर्वभावानां सामान्यं वृद्धिकारणं। ह्रासहेतुर्विशेषश्च, प्रवृत्तिरुभयस्य तु।।
chapters.summary: This foundational chapter establishes the essential concepts of Ayurveda including the definition of life (Ayu), health (Arogya), and the fourfold aims of human existence. It explains the three bodily doshas (Vata, Pitta, Kapha) and two mental doshas (Rajas, Tamas), the six basic principles of knowledge, and the theory of similarity and dissimilarity. The chapter provides detailed classification of medicinal substances including plant-based drugs (roots, fruits, latex, bark), animal products, and minerals. It lists specific drugs used for purification therapies (Shodhana), including sixteen roots, eight types of urine, eight types of milk, and five salts. The chapter emphasizes the importance of a qualified physician, ethical medical practice, and the rational use of medicines. It also describes the historical origins of Ayurvedic knowledge through the lineage from Brahma to Indra to Bharadwaja to Atreya and his six disciples, with Agnivesha creating the first comprehensive text.

chapters.englishName: Dehusked Seeds of Apamarga and Other Medicines
chapters.abstract: The second chapter within Bheshaja Chatushka (tetrad constituting four chapters on medicinal treatment) deals with list of herbs used in Panchakarma (bio-purification processes). The liberty to execute this treatment based upon dose and time of administration is given through logical reasoning (Yukti pramana). Specific diet preparations like gruels (Yavagu) are enlisted with their benefits and indications to be used in preservation of health and treatment of diseases. The chapter denotes importance of body purification and diet in healthcare system.
importantVerses: Verse 15: तान्युपस्थितदोषाणां स्नेहस्वेदोपपादनैः। पञ्चकर्माणि कुर्वीत मात्राकालौ विचारयन्।।
Verse 16: मात्राकालाश्रया युक्तिः, सिद्धिर्युक्तौ प्रतिष्ठिता। तिष्ठत्युपरि युक्तिज्ञो द्रव्यज्ञानवतां सदा।।
chapters.summary: This chapter focuses on herbs and medicines used in Panchakarma therapies. It provides detailed lists of drugs for Shirovirechana (nasal cleansing), Vamana (therapeutic emesis), Virechana (therapeutic purgation), and Basti (enema). The chapter emphasizes the importance of proper dose (Matra), time (Kala), and rational application (Yukti) in therapy. It also describes various medicated gruels (Yavagu) - 28 types - prepared with different herbs for specific diseases. These gruels are categorized as Ahara-pradhana (diet-centric) or Aushadha-pradhana (medication-centric). The chapter includes formulations for digestive disorders, diarrhea, blood disorders, worm infestations, thirst, weight management, respiratory diseases, and many other conditions. It concludes with qualities of an ideal physician who should possess good memory, knowledge of etiology, self-restraint, and presence of mind.

chapters.abstract: While the preceding chapter (Apamarga Tanduliya) dealt with internal application of therapies in the form of Panchakarma, this chapter deals with the external application of medications. Thirty two types of external applications are enlisted in this chapter. The important indication is Kushtha (Skin diseases). These are systemic disorders considered as major disease (maharaoga). They require internal cleansing and purification treatments prior to external treatments – and hence, the sequence of the chapters. Without prior internal treatment, local treatments have limited efficacy.
importantVerses: Verse 3-7: Listing of six formulations for Kushtha
Verse 30: Summary verse - इहात्रिजः सिद्धतमानुवाच द्वात्रिंशतं सिद्धमहर्षिपूज्यः। चूर्णप्रदेहान् विविधामयघ्नानारग्वधीये जगतो हितार्थम्।।
chapters.summary: This chapter deals with external applications of medicines, particularly for skin diseases (Kushtha). It describes 32 types of Churna Pradeha (powder pastes) prepared with various herbs and processed with different media like ghee, oil, milk, buttermilk, or cow urine. The three main types of external applications are Pralepa (thin cold paste for Pitta-Rakta), Pradeha (thick paste - cold for Pitta-Rakta, hot for Vata-Kapha), and Alepa (medium consistency). The chapter provides detailed formulations for treating various skin conditions including Kushtha (leprosy/skin diseases), Kilasa (leucoderma), Kitibha (psoriasis), Dadru (ringworm), Bhagandara (fistula), Arsha (piles), and Pama (papular eruptions). It also covers treatments for Vata disorders, Vatarakta (gout), headaches, pain in flanks, and body odor. The chapter emphasizes that skin diseases are systemic disorders requiring internal purification before external treatments for effective results.

chapters.abstract: This chapter provides details of fifty Mahakashaya (or five classes of groups of ten medicines, and six hundred evacuatives) to be used in various diseases. Overall, this Chatushka provides a list of drugs to be used in various forms in a variety of diseases.
chapters.summary: This chapter details the classifications of medicinal groups used in Ayurveda. It covers the concept of Mahakashaya - groups of ten therapeutic agents - and provides comprehensive lists of drugs used for various purification procedures. The chapter explains different types of evacuative therapies (Virechana) and their applications in disease management. It serves as a reference for selecting appropriate drugs based on the disease condition, dosha involvement, and patient constitution. The knowledge presented in this chapter completes the Bheshaja Chatushka by providing extensive pharmacopeial knowledge essential for Ayurvedic practice.

chapters.englishName: Proper Quantity of Food and Daily Regimen
chapters.abstract: The second tetrad is the Swastha Chatushka that deals with important guidelines to be followed by healthy individuals to maintain their health. The first chapter of this tetrad, Matrashiteeya, deals with the daily regimen to be followed by healthy individuals to maintain their health.
chapters.summary: This chapter deals with daily regimen (Dinacharya) and proper quantity of food (Matra) for maintaining health. It provides detailed guidelines for daily activities including morning routine (Brahma Muhurta), oil massage (Abhyanga), exercise (Vyayama), bathing, meals, sleep, and other daily practices. The chapter emphasizes the importance of proper quantity (Matra) in food and medicine, explaining both under-use and over-use can be harmful. It describes the eight factors of food (Ashta Ahara Vidhi Visheshayatana) including source (Desha), time (Kala), processing (Pravicharana), combination (Samyoga), quantity (Matra), container (Patra), and proper use (Upayoga). The chapter provides the foundation for Swasthavritta (preventive healthcare) in Ayurveda.

chapters.abstract: The second chapter, Tasyashiteeya, recommends changes one should make in his/her daily habits and lifestyle i.e. clothing, food habits, exercise etc., depending upon the season, to stay healthy.
chapters.summary: This chapter describes Ritucharya - the seasonal regimen for maintaining health. It explains how one should modify diet, lifestyle, clothing, exercise, and therapeutic procedures according to six seasons: Summer (Grishma), Monsoon (Varsha), Autumn (Sharad), Winter (Hemanta), Late Winter (Shishira), and Spring (Vasanta). The chapter details the characteristic features of each season, the predominant dosha in each season, and the recommended diet and lifestyle modifications. It emphasizes that seasonal regimens help maintain the balance of doshas and prevent diseases. The chapter also explains the concept of Ritu Sandhi (junction between seasons) and the importance of gradual transition between seasonal regimens.

chapters.abstract: The third chapter, Naveganadharaniya, explains the importance of suppressible and non-suppressible urges in the human body, diseases due to non-suppressible urges and their treatment.
chapters.summary: This chapter explains the management of natural urges (Vega). It categorizes urges into suppressible (Dharaniya) and non-suppressible (Adharaniya) types. Non-suppressible urges that should not be controlled include hunger, thirst, vomiting, sneezes, tears, etc. The chapter describes diseases that occur from suppressing these natural urges and their treatments. The chapter emphasizes that suppression of natural urges leads to various disorders and proper management is essential for maintaining health.

chapters.abstract: Indriyopakramaniya, the last chapter of Swastha Chatushka, deals with sadvritta (general code of conduct). Besides maintaining his own health, sadvritta also helps the individual in maintaining healthy relations with other individuals, thus helping maintain harmony in the society at large.
chapters.summary: This chapter deals with the care of sense organs and the code of conduct (Sadvritta) for maintaining physical and mental health. It describes the proper care of five sensory organs: eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and skin. The chapter emphasizes the importance of ethical conduct, mental discipline, and social harmony in maintaining health. It includes guidelines for personal hygiene, social behavior, and spiritual practices that contribute to overall well-being.

chapters.abstract: The first chapter Khuddakachatushpad, deals with four aspects of therapeutics) - vaidya (physician), dravya (medicine), upasthata (caretaker) and rogi (patient). Four qualities of each of these aspects and prime importance of the physician among all of them.
chapters.summary: This chapter describes the four essential aspects of therapeutics: physician (Vaidya), medicine (Dravya), caretaker (Upasthata), and patient (Rogi). It enumerates the qualities required for each component. The physician should have thorough knowledge of the patient, disease, and therapeutics. The medicine should be appropriate, authentic, and properly processed. The caretaker should be skilled, attentive, and dedicated. The patient should be cooperative, follow instructions, and have faith in the physician. The chapter emphasizes that the physician is the most important among these four as he coordinates all aspects of treatment.

chapters.abstract: The next chapter, Mahachatushpada, explains the classification of diseases on the basis of prognosis. It is recommended in this chapter that the treatment should only be initiated after thorough diagnosis and identification of the disease, and the physician should refrain himself from treating the incurable diseases.
chapters.summary: This chapter expands on the four aspects of therapeutics with greater detail, particularly focusing on disease classification and prognosis. It explains how diseases should be classified based on curability: easily curable (Sukha Sadhya), curable with difficulty (Krichhra Sadhya), manageable (Yapya), and incurable (Asadhya). The chapter stresses the importance of proper diagnosis before initiating treatment and advises physicians to avoid treating incurable diseases. It also describes communicable diseases (Aupsargika) and diseases caused by single or multiple doshas.

chapters.abstract: The third chapter, Tistraishaniya deals with topics such as the three types of desires, strength, causes of diseases, their types, pathways, physicians, and therapies.
chapters.summary: This chapter discusses the three fundamental human desires (Tistraishani): desire for longevity, wealth, and happiness. It explains three types of strength: Daiva (divine/providential), Yuktikrita (acquired through rational means), and Yukta (natural/congenital). The chapter covers the causes of diseases, their classification, pathways of disease development, types of physicians, and various therapeutic approaches.

chapters.abstract: The last chapter of Nirdesha Chatushka, Vatakalakaliya deals with the good and bad qualities/functions of vata, pitta, and kapha. A physician should have a thorough knowledge of the guidelines provided in this tetrad to succeed in his field.
chapters.summary: This chapter provides a detailed study of the three doshas: Vata, Pitta, and Kapha. It describes their normal functions (Physiological) and abnormal functions (Pathological) in the body. The chapter explains the qualities and actions of each dosha, their roles in maintaining health, and how their imbalance leads to diseases. A physician must have thorough knowledge of doshas to diagnose and treat diseases effectively.

chapters.abstract: The first chapter, Snehadhyaya, provides the guidelines for proper use of sneha (lipids) either for shodhana or for shamana (to appease/palliation) purposes. A patient who has successfully completed the snehana procedure is now subjected to swedana procedure.
chapters.summary: This chapter provides comprehensive guidelines for oleation therapy (Snehana). It covers types of sneha (ghee, oil, vasa, majja), methods of administration (internal and external), indications, contraindications, and complications. The chapter distinguishes between shamana sneha (for pacification) and shodhana sneha (for purification). It provides detailed procedures for internal oleation including proper dose, time of administration, and accompanying diet.

chapters.abstract: The next chapter, Swedadhyaya, explains the various types of swedana (fomentation) recommended for various diseases. Snehana and swedana help the toxins to move towards the gut from where they will be expelled out of the body either through vamana (therapeutic emesis) or virechana (therapeutic purgation).
chapters.summary: This chapter describes various types of fomentation therapy (Swedana). It explains the indications, methods, and contraindications of different types of swedana including nadi sweda (tubal), pinda sweda (bolus), avagaha sweda (drench), and others. The chapter emphasizes that swedana helps mobilize toxins towards the gastrointestinal tract for elimination through purification therapies (vamana or virechana).

chapters.abstract: The next chapter, Upakalpaniya, emphasizes on how a physician should be well equipped before administering any shodhana procedure to any of the patients. This chapter provides the outline for a fully equipped hospital and standard vamana and virechana procedures.
chapters.summary: This chapter provides detailed guidelines for preparing the patient and facility for Panchakarma therapies. It describes the pre-operative (Purva Karma), main procedure (Pradhana Karma), and post-operative (Paschat Karma) protocols. The chapter outlines requirements for a well-equipped healthcare facility and standard procedures for vamana and virechana therapies.

chapters.abstract: The last chapter of this tetrad, Chikitsaprabhritiya, depicts the importance of shodhana over shamana therapy. The details of properly / improperly administered shodhana procedures are discussed here. Important concepts like shuddha chikitsa (pure form of treatment)and svabhavoparamavada (theory of natural destruction) etc. have also been described in this chapter.
chapters.summary: This chapter emphasizes the importance of purification therapies (Shodhana) over pacification (Shamana). It discusses proper and improper administration of purification treatments, complications, and their management. The chapter introduces concepts like Shuddha Chikitsa (pure treatment) and Svabhavoparamavada (natural destruction theory). It guides physicians on when to choose purification versus pacification therapies.

chapters.abstract: The first chapter Kiyanta Shiraseeya provides the details of diseases like shiroroga (diseases of the head), hridroga (cardiac diseases), eighteen types of kshaya (loss of body tissues), vidradhi (abscess) and madhumeha (a clinical condition similar to diabetes mellitus).
chapters.summary: This chapter covers diseases of the head and neck region including Shiroroga (head diseases), Hridroga (cardiac diseases), various types of tissue loss (Kshaya), Vidradhi (abscess), and Madhumeha (diabetes). It provides classification and characteristics of eighteen types of Kshaya (tissue depletion) conditions.

chapters.abstract: The next chapter, Trishothiya, elucidates various types of edema.
chapters.summary: This chapter provides detailed information about various types of edema (Shotha). It classifies edema based on dosha involvement: Vataja, Pittaja, Kaphaja, and Tridoshaja. The chapter discusses etiology, symptoms, and treatment approaches for different types of swelling.

chapters.abstract: The third chapter, Ashtodariya, reveals the types of about 48 diseases that are caused by a combination of doshas.
chapters.summary: This chapter describes eighteen types of diseases caused by various combinations of doshas. It explains diseases arising from dual dosha involvement (Vata-Pitta, Vata-Kapha, Pitta-Kapha) and triple dosha involvement (Sannipata). The chapter provides a comprehensive understanding of combinational disease pathologies.

chapters.abstract: The last chapter, Maharoga, is exclusively dedicated to the diseases caused by single dosha (vata, pitta, or kapha).
chapters.summary: This chapter is dedicated to diseases caused by single dosha: Vataja, Pittaja, and Kaphaja disorders. It provides detailed understanding of how individual doshas when vitiated lead to specific disease manifestations. The chapter serves as a foundation for understanding disease classification based on dosha involvement.

chapters.abstract: The first chapter of this tetrad, Ashtauninditiya, describes eight types of people who are marginalized (or ridiculed) in the society due to their physical features. Out of these eight, only two i.e. atisthoola (morbidly obese) and atikrisha (emaciated) are described in detail because of their clinical significance along with their symptomatology and treatment.
chapters.summary: This chapter describes eight types of socially marginalized individuals due to physical deformities or conditions. It provides detailed focus on two clinically significant conditions: obesity (Atisthoola) and emaciation (Atikrisha), including their etiology, symptoms, and treatment approaches.

chapters.abstract: The next chapter, Langhanabrimhaniya, describes six types of treatment i.e. langhana (fasting), brimhana (nourishing therapy), snehana, swedana, rukshana (medical treatment for reducing fat) and stambhana (astringent therapy) – primarily for managing atisthoola or atikrisha conditions, but also indicated for various other conditions described later in the Samhita. Out of these six, mainly two therapies i.e. langhana and brimhana have been described in greater detail.
chapters.summary: This chapter describes six therapeutic modalities: Langhana (fasting), Brimhana (nourishing), Snehana (oleation), Swedana (fomentation), Rukshana (drying), and Stambhana (astringent). The chapter provides detailed guidance on fasting and nourishing therapies for managing obesity and emaciation.

chapters.abstract: The third chapter, Santarpaniya deals with diseases caused due to over-nourishment or under-nourishment along with their treatment.
chapters.summary: This chapter deals with disorders arising from over-nourishment (Santarpaniya) and under-nourishment (Apatarpaniya). It explains the pathophysiology, symptoms, and treatment of nutritional disorders.

chapters.abstract: The last chapter of this Chatushka, Vidhishonitiya, deals with diseases that are not cured by any of the above-mentioned therapies and termed as diseases due to vitiation of rakta (blood). Such diseases, along with their etiology, symptomatology and treatment have been described in this chapter.
chapters.summary: This chapter addresses blood disorders (Rakta Dushti) that are not cured by standard therapies. It covers diseases arising from blood vitiation, their etiology, symptoms, and treatment approaches.

chapters.abstract: The first chapter, Yajjah Purushiya brings forth the important perspective of the origin of human beings and the origin of diseases. This chapter also describes 155 entities (Agrya, or entities considered best in their category of drugs, food articles, bio-purification procedures, etc.)that are important for healthy as well as diseased individuals.
chapters.summary: This chapter explores the origin of human beings and diseases. It introduces the concept of 155 best entities (Agrya) - the best in their category of drugs, food articles, and purification procedures - essential for both healthy and diseased individuals.

chapters.abstract: The next chapter Atreyabhadrakapyiya, describes in detail the concept of Ayurvedic pharmacology in the form of rasa (taste), veerya (drug potency), and vipaka (final conversion of food/drug after the action of jatharagni (digestive power) and prabhava (specific action of a drug). This chapter also throws light on the important concept of viruddha ahara (incompatible diet) which seems to be the primary cause of many diseases even today.
chapters.summary: This chapter is a foundational text on Ayurvedic pharmacology. It explains the concepts of Rasa (taste), Veerya (potency), Vipaka (post-digestive effect), and Prabhava (specific action). The chapter emphasizes the importance of Viruddha Ahara (incompatible food combinations) as a cause of many diseases.

chapters.abstract: The third chapter, Annapanavidhi Adhyaya provides details of Ayurvedic dietetics. This chapter details a wide variety of food and beverages, along with their medicinal values.
chapters.summary: This chapter provides comprehensive information on Ayurvedic dietetics. It describes various food items including cereals, milk products, meats, beverages, and their medicinal properties. The chapter serves as a guide for dietary recommendations in health and disease.

chapters.abstract: The last chapter, Vividhashitapitiya deals with important concepts such as formation of body tissues from the diet consumed, immunity and immune-compromised individuals, diseases originated from various body tissues, and migration of dosha from shakha (periphery or the tissue elements) to koshtha (central part of the body or alimentary tract) and vice versa.
chapters.summary: This chapter explains the formation of body tissues (Dhatu) from food, concepts of immunity (Oja), and diseases arising from various tissues. It also discusses the migration of doshas between peripheral (Shakha) and central (Koshtha) parts of the body.

chapters.abstract: The first of these two chapters, Dashapranayataneeya deals with the ten locations in the human body where Prana (life) resides. Besides this important concept, the chapter also details the attributes of a pranabhisaravaidya (a physician who protects the life) and a rogabhisaravaidya (a physician who aggravates the disease and takes away the life of the patient).
chapters.summary: This chapter describes the ten vital points (Dashapranayatana) where life force (Prana) resides. It outlines the qualities of an ideal physician (Pranabhisara Vaidya) who protects life and contrasts it with an incompetent physician (Rogabhisara Vaidya) who harms patients.

chapters.abstract: The last chapter, Arthedashmahamooliya deals with a variety of subjects such as the importance of Arth (hridaya-heart), ten major blood vessels or channels from the heart, the definition of Ayu (combination of four entities i.e. body, mind, soul and senses) and its four types, Ayurveda, the aim of Ayurvedic science, and its method of study etc.
chapters.summary: This final chapter covers multiple fundamental concepts including the importance of the heart (Hridaya), eleven fundamental roots (Arthedashmahamoola), ten major blood vessels, and the definition of life (Ayu) comprising body, mind, soul, and senses. It summarizes the aims of Ayurvedic science and methods of study.
